title: 802.11 a/b/g/n/ac/ax standards and the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands

videos.script: Every lesson so far had a cable, even if the cable was virtual. This one has none, and neither does the lab. {{no-radio}} The lab is one computer with virtual Ethernet between its machines. There is no radio in it, so nothing in this lesson is a capture. The numbers come from the standards, and from arithmetic you can run yourself. {{numbers}} Wi-Fi is one IEEE standard, 802.11, and a series of amendments to it. Each amendment made it faster, and the industry later gave the main ones plain names. Wi-Fi 4, 5, 6 and 7. {{names}} They work in three bands of radio frequency. Two point four, five and six gigahertz. The lowest band reaches furthest. The higher two have far more room. {{bands}} Wider channels, more antennas and better ways of sharing make the number on the box bigger. {{rate}} But that number is not what a phone downloads at. The air is shared, one speaker at a time. And one slow client can take most of a channel's time. {{airtime}} By the end, you will read a product sheet and know which of its numbers you will actually see. {{sheet}}
